quarterly_data.signal: Q4 2025 results: total company revenue increased 19.4% year over year (KTS and Sigma and Omega acquisitions plus organic growth); Q4 adjusted EPS grew 25% to $1.88 and full-year adjusted EPS grew 21% to $6.76, with full-year adjusted EBITDA also up 21%. HVAC segment Q4 revenue grew 16.4% (5.5% inorganic, 10.3% organic, with solid growth in both cooling and heating); HVAC segment income grew 18% and segment margin rose 40 basis points on higher volume and operating leverage. HVAC segment backlog at year end was $585,000,000, up 22% organically year over year.
quarterly_data.figure: Q4 revenue +19.4%; Q4 adj. EPS $1.88 (+25%); full-year adj. EPS $6.76 (+21%); HVAC Q4 revenue +16.4% (organic 10.3%); HVAC backlog up 22% organically

quarterly_data.signal: Initial FY2026 guidance (includes the Thermalek and Air Enterprises / Ron Industries acquisitions; Crawford United's industrial and transportation products businesses are excluded as discontinued operations): total company revenue $2,535,000,000 to $2,605,000,000; segment income margin 24.6% to 25.1%; adjusted EBITDA $590,000,000 to $620,000,000 (approximately 20% growth and a margin of approximately 23.5% at the midpoint) and adjusted EPS $7.60 to $8.00 (approximately 15% growth at the midpoint). HVAC segment revenue $1,800,000,000 to $1,840,000,000 with segment margin 24.5% to 25%; the HVAC margin guide carries temporary start-up costs for the new plants of around a 50 basis point impact. The acquisitions add about $35,000,000 of annual revenue at Thermalek and the low $80,000,000s for Air Enterprises and Ron combined (just shy of about $110,000,000 for eleven months of ownership), at segment income margins slightly above the segment average. Non-data center, non-custom air handling parts of HVAC are expected to grow low single digits. HVAC strength: data centers, healthcare, power, heavy industrial, aftermarket and institutional/higher ed; softer for 2026: battery automotive, semiconductor, chemical and commercial real estate. First-half / second-half cadence expected to be similar to the prior year, with capacity-expansion benefits more evident in the back half.

Data center exposure (initial 2026 view): the CEO said 2025 data center revenue was about 9% of company revenue (versus a 7% figure given previously), in the neighborhood of $200,000,000, 'maybe a little bit more'; for 2026 he expects data centers to be low double digits of revenue, 'say, 12%', with data center growth 'probably in the 50% neighborhood'. Several hyperscalers are pushing for acceleration, and demand with existing customers and in new bid situations remains very robust.
quarterly_data.figure: 2025 data center revenue in the neighborhood of $200,000,000 (about 9% of revenue); 2026 data center growth probably in the 50% neighborhood (low double digits, say, 12% of revenue)

quarterly_data.signal: Capacity expansion plan (as of Q4 2025): expansions at existing HVAC facilities (including Ingenia and the Cooling Products Olathe location) plus two new facilities should add roughly $700,000,000 of incremental capacity once at full production - about $550,000,000 for data center and about $150,000,000 for custom air handling, predominantly Ingenia - and enable nearly half of the HVAC segment's 2026 revenue growth. Full production capacity on the two new expansions is expected sometime in 2028; management saw no imminent need for additional expansion in the next couple of years but would evaluate opportunities if demand accelerates.
quarterly_data.figure: roughly $700,000,000 incremental capacity at full production (about $550,000,000 data center, about $150,000,000 custom air handling); full production sometime in 2028

quarterly_data.signal: New plants and expansion capex: in Q4 2025 SPX completed the purchase of a 459,000 square foot facility in Madison, Alabama with flexible manufacturing for custom air handling and data center solutions, including the new Olympus Max - assembly only in the second half of 2026, not in a production phase until 2027. A new Tennessee facility for Tamco highly engineered aluminum dampers (seeing strong data center demand) was to come online at the end of Q1 2026 and ramp through the year; ramps are partly driven by equipment lead times. Expansion-related investment across HVAC facilities is expected to require approximately $100,000,000 of capital in 2026, in addition to approximately $60,000,000 invested in 2025; timing of equipment deliveries is the primary swing factor for the capex plan.
quarterly_data.figure: Madison, Alabama 459,000 square foot facility; expansion capital approximately $100,000,000 in 2026 (approximately $60,000,000 in 2025)

quarterly_data.signal: Olympus Max dry / adiabatic cooler: the CEO said 'we have a winner here' and he feels more bullish than on the prior call, citing advantages on tonnage and flexibility (the dry unit can be upgraded to an adiabatic after the fact), integrated controls as a differentiator versus competitors, and more robust mechanical equipment. SPX has been awarded with three customers in material amounts, hit its target of $50,000,000 of bookings last year and is converting that to revenue this year; one customer has already locked up multiple years of growing demand, and management feels good looking to 2027, 2028 and 2029.
quarterly_data.figure: $50,000,000 Olympus Max bookings target met last year; awarded with three customers

quarterly_data.signal: NVIDIA Rubin read-through: the CEO said Rubin's ability to run at lower water temperatures raised concern about whether chillers are needed - some designs may need fewer or no chillers - but he is not aware of circumstances where the Rubin chip would reduce the need for external heat rejection, where SPX plays, so Rubin 'really has no negative impact on us' and has some positive impact in architectures seen. Higher-power AI chips generate more heat, requiring more cooling towers (adiabatic, dry or normal Marley). The bulk of the data center market has historically used air-cooled chillers, where SPX does not really participate; as heat loads get bigger the market is moving toward water-cooled chilling and free cooling, which are attractive opportunities for SPX. On higher-voltage architectures he said kW per rack and data center electricity are not decreasing, gigawatt-scale data centers need massive electricity, and electricity correlates to the amount of cooling needed.

Hyperscaler order visibility: SPX works with a set of hyperscalers with different methodologies - some lock SPX up for four or five years with very clear visibility on future demand; others lay out the plan and release POs on a more quarterly basis while vigorously validating SPX's capacity and quality. Management expects nice growth into 2027 and 2028, said lead times have not really changed, and noted large data center customers give much more visibility because cooling is mission critical. Separately, speaking about HVAC end markets overall (not data centers specifically), the CEO said bookings had a nice start at the end of Q4 and in the first seven weeks of this year.

Supply chain and costs: management said nothing across its supply chain is a material concern and a line-item-by-line-item bill-of-materials review showed no red flags for scaling up. Tariffs were not a material impact in 2025 (largely offset through price, sourcing and CI initiatives); the model is largely U.S., largely in-country-for-country sourcing, with Canadian businesses covered under USMCA, and because a large part of HVAC is configured or engineered to order there are no long lead-time exposures for steel and aluminum.
